title: The Place of Therapeutic Apheresis in Severe Immune-Related Adverse Events: A Scoping Review of Literature.
authors: Vuillet C, Moranne O, Daubin D et al.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the management of patients with cancer. However, they can induce breakdowns in immunologic tolerance, leading to autoimmune diseases, or immune related adverse events (irAEs). These irAEs can sometimes be life threatening, requiring aggressive management, such as immunosuppressant (IS) or even therapeutic apheresis (TA). TA, an extracorporeal circulation technique, may represent a therapeutic option for severe irAEs, reducing their severity and duration by removing ICIs, pathogenic antibodies or inflammatory cytokines, although its role in this situation remains underreported. We made scoping review to better identify the use of TA for managing severe irAEs. From January 2022 to August 2025, three databases were reviewed, for articles mentioning the use of TA in the event of immunotoxicity. Only case reports or case series were retained. A descriptive summary was produced in table forms. Between 2022 and 2025, 162 articles were identified, 34 articles concerning 42 patients treated for severe irAE via TA were included. The underlying cancers were mainly non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma, and 78% of patients were treated with monotherapy anti-PD(L)1. The main indications for TA were neurological (40.6%), overlap manifestations (23.8%), and hepatitis (21.4%), mainly highly severe. TA was most often used in rescue situations, that is, after failure of several lines of IS. Complications of TA were rare. Clinical improvement was reported in most patients, usually within days of TA, with 24% complete resolution, and 45% partial resolution. Despite revolutionizing cancer treatment, ICIs induce severe irAEs, with poorly defined therapeutic options. TA may be a therapeutic option for life threatening irAEs, with data in the literature assuming its effectiveness. However, details on its use remain poorly defined. Further studies are required to emphasize its use as in irAEs.

title: Immune composition and adenosine-associated transcription in non-small-cell lung cancer after neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade.
authors: Chen LZ, Chen RN, Wen GA
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), high metabolic gene expression during immunotherapy can reflect either more infiltrating cells or altered cellular activity. We tested whether separating cell abundance from cell-intrinsic transcription clarifies incomplete tumour clearance after neoadjuvant programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) blockade.
METHODS: Using cross-dataset triangulation, we analysed 1173,843 post-treatment immune cells from 224 patients (103 non-major pathological response [non-MPR], 40 major response, and 81 complete response) via patient-level regressions adjusted for clinical covariates, cell proportions, and library size. Findings were compared across recurrence follow-up (n = 154), spatial profiling (n = 40), three bulk cohorts (n = 78), population data (n = 3045), and 7224 genetic tests.
RESULTS: Non-MPR tumours had higher regulatory T-cell (Treg) proportions (+3.91% FOXP3+, +3.07% CCR8+) and elevated lymphoid glycolysis, exhaustion, Treg, and adenosine scores (all false-discovery rate q ≤ 1.09 × 10-7). Notably, adjusting for cell composition and depth abolished broad glycolysis and exhaustion differences, whereas adenosine-associated transcription persisted (difference 0.044, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.020-0.068; q = 0.0046), peaking in terminally exhausted CD8+ T cells (0.449, 95% CI 0.328-0.571; q = 1.29 × 10-10). Paired spatial biopsies localized HK2, LDHB, and SLC16A1 to tumour regions (q ≤ 0.0057) and CTLA4 to stroma (q = 5.14 × 10-5) without response interactions. A six-component score discriminated non-MPR (apparent area under the curve [AUC] 0.791, 95% CI 0.724-0.851) and recurrence (hazard ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.04-1.93), attenuating after pathology adjustment, but failed in pre-treatment bulk cohorts (AUCs 0.091-0.517); no genetic test passed correction (q ≥ 0.9934).
CONCLUSIONS: Incomplete response involves Treg accumulation and cell-intrinsic adenosine transcription, offering exploratory, hypothesis-generating insights for prospective validation.

title: Routes to diagnosis and survival in Danish patients with non-small cell lung cancer: the impact of emergency admission.
authors: Christensen NL, Kristensen K, Rasmussen TR et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Worldwide, lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related death. Studies have shown that receiving a lung cancer diagnosis following an unplanned admission is associated with poor prognosis. The causal relationship between emergency presentation and survival remains uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a population-based retrospective study including a random sample of 1,000 Danish patients diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) between 2014 and 2016, identified through the Danish Lung Cancer Registry. Detailed data on route to diagnosis, stage, performance status, comorbidity, and survival were retrieved from electronic health records. Associations between route to diagnosis and survival were examined using logistic regression adjusted for relevant clinical covariates.
RESULTS: Of 974 eligible patients, 234 (24%) were diagnosed following emergency admission. These patients were more likely to present with advanced stage (stage IV: 70% vs. 43%) and have poorer performance status. One- and five‑year survival were markedly lower in patients admitted acutely (32% and 8%) compared to non-emergency presenters (56% and 22%; p < 0.001). The adjusted odds ratio for 5-year survival following emergency admission was 0.47 (95% CI 0.28-0.81). After adjusting for disease stage, emergency admission was no longer independently associated with survival.
CONCLUSION: Approximately one in four Danish patients with NSCLC were diagnosed following emergency admission. This route was strongly associated with advanced stage and poor prognosis, suggesting that emergency admission reflects late-stage disease rather than being an independent prognostic factor. Efforts to reduce diagnosis following emergency admission should focus on early detection, improved symptom awareness, and optimized diagnostic pathways.

title: Cellular origins and evolutionary dynamics of plasma cfDNA in solid tumors: integrating germline, tumor-derived, and hematopoietic variation for MRD and treatment guidance.
authors: Zhao Q, Wu C, Huang X et al.
abstract: Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a heterogeneous and rapidly changing biological pool derived from malignant cells, normal tissues, and hematopoietic cells. The abundance and molecular composition of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) are determined not only by tumor burden but also by tissue architecture, vascular access, cell-death programs, chromatin organization, nuclease processing, systemic clearance, treatment exposure, and clonal evolution. These biological determinants shape the mutation, methylation, fragmentation, nucleosomal, and temporal features exploited by contemporary liquid-biopsy assays. Accurate clinical interpretation therefore requires both sensitive detection and reliable source attribution, particularly the distinction of tumor-derived variants from constitutional germline alterations and clonal hematopoiesis. In this review, we integrate the biological origins and processing of plasma cfDNA with analytical strategies for low-tumor-fraction detection and critically evaluate the evidence supporting postoperative molecular residual disease (MRD), recurrence surveillance, treatment-response assessment, resistance monitoring, and ctDNA-guided therapy across solid tumors. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing prognostic validity, treatment-predictive value, and demonstrated clinical utility. Current evidence is strongest in colorectal cancer and, more recently, ctDNA-selected urothelial cancer, whereas routine ctDNA-directed intervention in resected non-small cell lung cancer and breast cancer remains insufficiently validated. By linking cfDNA biology to an explicit hierarchy of clinical evidence, this review defines both the established applications and the major limitations that must be addressed before broader implementation of ctDNA-guided precision oncology.

title: Minimal Ablative Margin as a Key Predictor of Local Tumor Progression After Percutaneous Lung Tumor Ablation.
authors: Chang CC, Hsiao HT, Chung TJ et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Minimally invasive local therapies such as radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA), and cryoablation (CA) are commonly used to treat malignant lung tumors. This study aimed to identify predictors of local tumor progression (LTP), focusing on the role of minimal ablative margin.
METHODS: The medical records of patients ≥ 20 years old with primary or metastatic lung tumors who underwent percutaneous ablation from July 2011 to December 2022 were retrospectively reviewed. Patient demographic information, tumor characteristics, and ablation details were extracted. The primary outcome was LTP, and the key variable of interest was the minimal ablative margin.
RESULTS: Seventy-one patients with 88 nodules ablated were included in the analysis, and 22% of the nodules exhibited LTP. In the overall cohort, ROC analysis identified 3 mm as the optimal cut-off for minimal ablative margin to predict LTP. Nodules with margins ≥ 3 mm were associated with significantly higher LTP-free survival at 5 years (82% vs. 23% margins < 3 mm). Kaplan-Meier analysis indicated a significant difference in LTP between ablative margins ≥ 3 and < 3 mm (p < 0.001). RFA was associated with a higher LTP risk than MWA (hazard ratio [HR] = 5.43, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.84-16.05), as was a margin < 3 mm (HR = 24.24, 95% CI: 7.66-76.71).
CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, achieving an ablative margin of at least 3 mm was associated with improved LTP-free survival after lung tumor ablation.
ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This threshold should be considered a pragmatic, context-dependent estimate that may require validation across ablation modalities and clinical settings.

title: Outcomes After Curative-intent Resection of Synchronous Primary Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC): Two is Worse than One.
authors: Seyoum N, Eaton DB, Brennan L et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Outcomes following curative-intent resection of synchronous primary lung cancer (SPLC) remain incompletely defined. We compared recurrence and survival in SPLC versus solitary primary tumors among patients with clinical stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of Veterans undergoing curative-intent resection for clinical stage I NSCLC in the Veterans Health Administration (2006-2020). SPLC was defined as two distinct clinical stage I NSCLC tumors diagnosed within six weeks, with curative-intent treatment of both tumors within one year. Propensity score matching (PSM) (1:1) was used to compare patients with SPLC to those with solitary tumors. The primary outcome was cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR); secondary outcomes were overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). Additional analyses examined the role of adjuvant treatment and drivers of recurrence in SPLC patients.
RESULTS: Of 12,606 Veterans with resected clinical stage I NSCLC, 337 (2.7%) had SPLC. SPLC presented with larger tumors and more advanced pathologic stage. Histology was discordant between the two tumors in 44.2% of SPLC cases. In the propensity-matched cohort (281 pairs), SPLC was associated with higher CIR (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.10-2.07), worse DFS (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.03-1.50), and worse OS (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.01-1.45). Within SPLC, wedge resection of both tumors was independently associated with recurrence.
CONCLUSIONS: After adjustment, SPLC was associated with higher recurrence and worse survival than solitary tumors, supporting recognition of SPLC as a higher-risk phenotype within clinical stage I NSCLC.

title: Prognostic impact of lung dose during radiotherapy on patients with lung cancer in the era of immunotherapy.
authors: Pang B, Liu E, Wang DH et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To assess the prognostic impact of lung dose on non-metastatic lung cancer patients in the era of immunotherapy.
METHODS: In this retrospective, single-institution study, 69 patients with non-metastatic lung cancer who received chest radiotherapy (RT) between October 2018 and July 2025 were enrolled, including 45 who received immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) prior to RT. Clinical characteristics, treatments, prognosis, and RT parameters were analyzed.
RESULTS: Of the 69 patients, 46.4% had a mean lung dose (MLD) ≤ 12 Gy. The 2-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate was significantly higher in the MLD ≤ 12 Gy group (80.8% vs. 38.1% for the MLD > 12 Gy group, P = 0.004). Overall survival (OS) rates were 95.8% vs. 48.2% (P = 0.001), and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) rates were 92.3% vs. 65.0% (P = 0.016). Thirty-two patients (46.4%) had a lung volume receiving ≤ 5 Gy (lung V5) ≤ 50%. Patients with a lung V5 ≤ 50% demonstrated significantly better 2-year PFS (79.2% vs. 40.4%, P = 0.002), OS (90.2% vs. 52.4%, P = 0.002), and DMFS (85.9% vs. 69.3%, P = 0.028). Multivariate analysis confirmed MLD as an independent predictor of PFS and OS. Among patients with an MLD > 12 Gy, the primary causes of death were tumor progression and pneumonitis.
CONCLUSIONS: MLD is an independent prognostic predictor in non-metastatic lung cancer. Careful attention to MLD is warranted to optimize survival outcomes and mitigate treatment-related toxicities in the era of immunotherapy.

title: Exploring Gut Microbial Metabolic Signatures Associated with the Gut-Lung Axis in Lung Adenocarcinoma.
authors: Yuan JQ, Zhong JY, Hu TC et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The gut-lung axis (GLA) is increasingly recognized as a biological communication pathway relevant to lung cancer. However, the potential molecular associations between gut microbial metabolites and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remain incompletely understood.
METHODS: By integrating public databases, including gutMGene, GeneCards, and TCGA, with computational tools such as WGCNA, STRING, and CIBERSORT, candidate genes and gut microbiota-derived metabolites potentially associated with LUAD were identified. A microbiota-metabolite-targets-pathway (MMTP) interaction network was constructed, followed by functional enrichment, immune infiltration analysis, miRNA-target prediction, and drug-likeness analyses.
RESULTS: Among the 12 key targets identified, JUN, IL6, and CXCL8 were prioritized as core genes. These targets mainly involved miRNA-related processes and immune pathways like IL-17 signaling, Toll-like receptor, and Th17 differentiation. Immune infiltration showed that core gene expression correlated with specific immune cell patterns, indicating inflammatory and immunosuppressive features of the tumor microenvironment (TME). The MMTP network further suggested that several gut microbial metabolites, including butyrate, propionate, acetate, succinate, 3-indolepropionic acid, and trimethylamine N-oxide, may be associated with core gene-related pathways. In silico drug-likeness and toxicity predictions indicated that these metabolites generally met basic Lipinski-based criteria; however, several predicted toxicity signals, particularly human hepatotoxicity, warrant cautious interpretation.
CONCLUSION: Key gut microbial metabolites may be linked to LUAD progression via inflammatory and immune pathways involving JUN, IL6, and CXCL8, along with miRNA regulatory processes. These findings offer a bioinformatics framework for understanding GLA-related molecular links in LUAD and may help find biomarkers or metabolites for further study.

title: Prognostic factors and treatment outcomes for malignant thymoma: A single-center retrospective analysis.
authors: Salimi B, Seifi S, Rostami P et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective study evaluated the clinicopathological features, treatment patterns, and prognostic factors influencing long-term outcomes in patients with thymoma and thymic carcinoma at our institution.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We reviewed the electronic medical records of all patients diagnosed with thymic malignancies between 2005 and 2024 at the National Research Institute of Tuberculosis and Lung Diseases in Tehran, Iran. Demographic data, clinical stage, histopathological classification, treatment modality, and survival outcomes were retrieved from the records. Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, and prognostic factors were assessed with Cox proportional hazards modeling.
RESULTS: A total of 52 patients were identified, including 23 women (44.2%) and 29 men (55.8%), with a median age at diagnosis of 60 years. Myasthenia gravis was present in 9.6% of cases. The estimated 5-year overall survival (OS) for the entire cohort was 53%. Survival differed markedly by histology: patients with thymoma had a 5-year OS of 69%, whereas those with thymic carcinoma had a 5-year OS of 35%. On univariate analysis, histological subtype ( P = 0.03) was significantly associated with OS.
CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that histological subtype is a key determinant of long-term survival in thymic malignancies, with thymoma demonstrating substantially better outcomes than thymic carcinoma. The results highlight the prognostic value of accurate histopathological classification and emphasize the critical role of surgical resection-particularly as part of a multimodality treatment strategy-in improving survival. Early diagnosis, precise staging, and individualized treatment planning remain essential to optimize outcomes for patients with these rare tumors.

title: Forkhead box N1 (FOXN1) in thymus and skin from molecular basis to clinical translation: a review.
authors: Tie W, Zeng M, Zheng J et al.
abstract: Forkhead box protein N1 (FOXN1) is a pivotal transcription factor governing the development of the immune system and cutaneous tissues. This comprehensive review systematically elucidates the molecular structural features of FOXN1, with a particular focus on its essential biological functions within the thymic and cutaneous microenvironments. Specifically, it details the intricate regulation of thymic epithelial cell differentiation, cellular aging, and tissue regeneration, alongside its distinct impacts on skin homeostasis, local metabolism, and accelerated wound repair. Building upon this foundational biology, the article explores the broad clinical phenotype spectrum associated with FOXN1 deficiency, outlining its diagnostic and therapeutic value in conditions such as immunodeficiency, chronic skin disorders, and thymic neoplasms. Furthermore, it highlights cutting-edge translational strategies reshaping regenerative medicine, including FOXN1-based organoid construction and innovative targeted protein delivery systems. Ultimately, this review aims to provide a systematic, multi-disciplinary reference for understanding the pathophysiological significance of FOXN1, effectively bridging basic laboratory insights with advanced clinical applications.

title: Thymoma-associated Anti-α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-iso xazolepropionic Acid Receptor Encephalitis with Polyspecific Autoantibodies: A Case Report and Literature Review.
authors: Tseng TY, Chu YC
abstract: Anti-α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) encephalitis is a rare, often paraneoplastic, cause of limbic encephalitis. The concurrent presentation of anti-AMPAR encephalitis alongside multiple autoimmune syndromes and antibodies is exceedingly uncommon. We describe a 62-year-old man with no significant past medical history who presented with a rapidly progressive 4-month history of cognitive decline and gait disturbance. Comprehensive evaluation revealed anti-AMPAR encephalitis, thymoma, subclinical myasthenia gravis, and autoimmune thyroiditis, demonstrating coexistence of multiple autoimmune disorders. Immunological assessment identified a complex polyspecific autoantibody profile, including anti-AMPAR2, anti-Titin, anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase 65, anti-anti-acetylcholine receptor, and anti-thyroid antibodies. Following aggressive immunotherapy and thymectomy, the patient experienced substantial neurological improvement. Anti-AMPAR encephalitis can coexist with multiple autoimmune disorders and diverse autoantibodies. Therefore, thorough antibody screening and tumor evaluation are essential to identify occult etiologies and to guide optimal therapeutic strategies.

title: Medullary epithelium-free areas in the rat thymus are specialized niches enriched for mature thymocytes and distinct stromal subsets.
authors: Sawanobori Y, Ogawa T
abstract: The thymic medulla provides the microenvironment for negative selection, late thymocyte maturation, and thymocyte egress, and is generally characterized by widespread distribution of medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs). In contrast, the rat thymic medulla contains medullary epithelium-free areas (mEFAs), but the cellular composition and functional significance of these regions remain unclear. Here, to address these questions, we combined spatial transcriptomic data with thymocyte and stromal scRNA-seq reference datasets using robust cell-type decomposition (RCTD) to characterize mEFAs. These analyses revealed that more mature phenotypes within the CD4SP, CD8SP, and regulatory T-cell lineages were preferentially localized in mEFAs, whereas immature SP subsets were enriched in medullary epithelium-containing areas. The newly identified rat thymic mesenchymal cell subsets TMC3 and TMC4 were also enriched in mEFAs. These subsets were broadly similar to mouse medullary fibroblasts but displayed distinct predicted interactions with SP thymocytes, including costimulatory molecule-receptor, chemokine-receptor, and ECM-integrin axes. In addition, venous endothelial cells (vECs) expressing portal endothelial cell markers were enriched in mEFAs. Spns2, which encodes a transporter that releases S1P from cells into the extracellular space, was preferentially expressed in both TMC4 and vEC subsets, suggesting that these cells may contribute to the formation of a local S1P gradient within mEFAs. These findings suggest that mEFAs may be specialized medullary niches associated with stromal organization, the localization of mature thymocytes, and thymic egress.

title: Prognostic associations of PD-L1 expression and BAP1 loss in pleural mesothelioma: a retrospective single-center cohort from Colombia.
authors: Brugés R, Carvajal C, Luna-Meza A et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evidence on the prognostic associations of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1) in pleural mesothelioma (PM) remains inconsistent, and joint data from Latin American cohorts are limited. We evaluated these biomarkers in a Colombian cohort.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center cohort included adults with histologically confirmed PM treated at the Instituto Nacional de Cancerología, Bogotá, from January 2011 through December 2023. PD-L1 was quantified using tumor proportion score (TPS), with ≥1% as the primary threshold; BAP1 was classified as retained or lost by nuclear immunoreactivity. Overall survival (OS) was measured from pathologic diagnosis to death. Event-free survival (EFS) was measured from diagnosis to first documented progression or death; patients without an event were censored at last contact. Kaplan-Meier methods and separate multivariable Cox models were used.
RESULTS: Sixty-seven patients were included; 60/67 (89.6%) had locally advanced or metastatic disease. PD-L1 TPS ≥1% was present in 26/67 (38.8%), and BAP1 loss in 47/61 evaluable tumors (77.0%). All 67 patients died. Median OS was 9.20 months (95% CI, 6.11-14.13), and median EFS was 6.51 months (95% CI, 5.49-9.13). PD-L1 TPS ≥1% was not clearly associated with OS (adjusted HR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.57-1.86) or EFS (adjusted HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 0.62-2.00). BAP1 loss also showed no clear adjusted association with OS (HR, 1.57; 95% CI, 0.78-3.16) or EFS (HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 0.82-3.33).
CONCLUSIONS: Neither PD-L1 TPS ≥1% nor BAP1 loss showed a clear adjusted association with survival. These jointly measured estimates extend the evidence from an underrepresented Latin American population but require external validation; the exploratory ≥5% and ≥10% analyses were based on only 14 and 7 patients, respectively.

title: STK11 Adnexal Tumor: Expanding the Spectrum of Female Genital Tumors in Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome.
authors: Mirkovic J
abstract: Serine-threonine kinase 11 (STK11) adnexal tumors are rare clinically aggressive neoplasms most commonly arising in the paratubal/paraovarian tissue. They are of uncertain histogenesis, characterized by STK11 genomic alterations, with a subset associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The spectrum of morphologic appearances is wide. Most commonly, cords and trabeculae in myxoid stroma are seen in addition to other components. They exhibit polyphenotypic immunoprofile with frequent expression of epithelial, mesothelial, sex cord, and smooth muscle marker desmin as well as hormone receptors, and loss of cytoplasmic STK11 expression.

title: Lineage-mixed neurodevelopmental programs in pediatric sarcomas nominate tumor-selective surface antigen pairs.
summary: Pediatric solid tumors have low mutational burden, frequent oncogenic gene fusions, and developmental origins in arrested progenitor cells. Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) could represent an ideal tool to assess whether these convergent biological features yield shared therapeutic vulnerabilities. However, while existing tools can extract gene expression programs for pan-tumor single-cell data, interpreting them requires domain expertise across many disciplines and diseases. Here, we analyzed a pan-pediatric scRNA-seq atlas of 266 patient- and xenograft-derived samples across 22 pediatric solid tumor types. To address the bottleneck between gene program identification and interpretation, we developed an AI agent framework built on off-the-shelf large language models (e.g., Gemini 2.5) to interpret gene expression programs at the level of human experts, but at much greater scale and speed. Our agent identified ectopic expression of neuronal marker genes as a unique feature of several fusion-driven sarcomas. This gene expression pattern resulted in tumor-specific co-expression of mixed mesenchymal/neuronal surface markers, providing a plausible therapeutic window to target these tumor types using emerging AND-gated therapeutic strategies, such as bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and bispecific CAR-T cells. As proof of principle, we nominated and validated STEAP1/NPTXR as a Ewing sarcoma candidate cell surface target pair. Together, this work delivers a pan-pediatric solid tumor scRNA-seq atlas, establishes a generalizable and accessible AI-based framework that complements existing single-cell methods by automating interpretation of pan-disease single-cell atlases, and nominates new bispecific ADC/CAR-T targets for catastrophic pediatric cancers.
